# Comparative Evaluation

This chapter brings together the results from all Stage 2 models - classical embeddings
(Word2Vec, FastText), fine-tuned compact LLMs for sentiment classification (TinyLlama 1.1B,
Gemma 2 2B), a fine-tuned LLM for topic classification (Qwen2.5-1.5B), and a domain-adapted
transformer embedding model (Gemma Embedding 300M) - and evaluates them on a common basis
across three dimensions: classification performance, computational cost, and interpretability.

## A Note on Label Quality

All sentiment models are evaluated against labels derived from
`cardiffnlp/twitter-roberta-base-sentiment-latest`, a RoBERTa model trained on Twitter data, while
our corpus consists of long-form AI media articles.
The F1 scores therefore reflect agreement with the labelling model rather than true sentiment
accuracy, which places a practical ceiling on all results and their interpretation.

Topic classification models are evaluated against labels produced by an upstream BERT-based
topic modelling pipeline. These labels are algorithmically derived, not manually annotated.
The reported metrics therefore measure agreement with the upstream topic model rather than
validated ground truth, which is an important caveat when interpreting absolute scores.

## Overall Results — Sentiment Classification

```{python}
#| label: summary-table
#| echo: true

import pandas as pd

summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Model": ["Word2Vec + LR", "FastText + LR",
    "TinyLlama 1.1B", "Gemma 2 2B"],
    "Type": ["Classical", "Classical", "Fine-tuned LLM", "Fine-tuned LLM"],
    "Macro-F1": [0.752, 0.745, 0.757, 0.761],
    "Training Time": ["~2 min", "~2 min", "~28 min", "~66 min"],
    "Hardware": ["CPU (local)", "CPU (local)", "A100 (cloud)", "A100 (cloud)"],
    "CO2 (g)": ["~0.2", "~0.2", "~65", "~125"],
})

summary["Macro-F1"] = summary["Macro-F1"].map("{:.3f}".format)

styled = (
    summary.style
    .set_properties(**{"text-align": "center"})
    .set_table_styles([
        {"selector": "th", "props": [("text-align", "center"),
        ("background-color", "#f0f0f0")]}
    ])
)
styled
```

## Key Findings — Sentiment Classification

**Classical embeddings are surprisingly competitive.** Word2Vec achieves 0.752 Macro-F1 - only
0.009 below the best model (Gemma 2 2B, 0.761) - while training in 2 minutes on a laptop CPU
with a CO2 footprint 625 times smaller than Gemma 2. For this specific task and dataset,
classical methods deliver near-equivalent performance at a fraction of the cost.

**Model size yields diminishing returns.** Doubling the parameter count from TinyLlama (1.1B)
to Gemma 2 (2B) improved Macro-F1 by only 0.004. The marginal gain does not justify the
2.4x increase in training time and energy consumption.

**All models struggle equally with minority classes.** Negative and positive sentiment both
score around F1 = 0.72 across all approaches, while neutral consistently scores ~0.83.
This pattern reflects the class imbalance in the dataset (neutral = 61%, positive = 24%,
negative = 15%) rather than model-specific weaknesses.

**The label quality ceiling matters.** Since sentiment labels were generated by a Twitter-trained
RoBERTa model applied to long-form journalism, the practical upper bound for any model on this
task is well below 1.0. The narrow spread of results (0.745–0.761) across very different
architectures suggests all models are approaching this ceiling.

## Topic Classification — Qwen2.5-1.5B

Qwen2.5-1.5B was fine-tuned for topic classification using LoRA adapters (4-bit quantisation,
r=16, 2 epochs on an A100 GPU). Because the task and labels differ from the sentiment
experiments, it is more appropriate to compare Qwen against the classical topic classification
baselines than against TinyLlama or Gemma 2.

### Baseline vs. Fine-Tuned Performance

Fine-tuning produced a very large absolute gain. Before task-specific training, the pretrained
Qwen2.5-1.5B model had near-random performance on topic classification: accuracy of 34.3% and
a Macro-F1 of only 0.081. After two epochs of LoRA fine-tuning, accuracy rose to 79.4% and
Macro-F1 reached 0.720. This delta illustrates how much a domain-general language model must
adapt before it can match even simple classical baselines on a structured classification task.

```{python}
#| label: qwen-baseline-vs-finetuned
#| echo: true

import pandas as pd

qwen_stages = pd.DataFrame({
    "Stage": ["Pretrained baseline", "Fine-tuned (LoRA, 2 epochs)"],
    "Accuracy": ["34.3%", "79.4%"],
    "Macro-F1": ["0.081", "0.720"],
})

styled_qwen = (
    qwen_stages.style
    .set_properties(**{"text-align": "center"})
    .set_table_styles([
        {"selector": "th", "props": [("text-align", "center"),
        ("background-color", "#f0f0f0")]}
    ])
)
styled_qwen
```

### Comparison Against Classical Topic Baselines

Despite the large improvement from fine-tuning, Qwen2.5-1.5B did not surpass the classical
embedding models on topic classification:

```{python}
#| label: topic-comparison-table
#| echo: true

import pandas as pd

topic_summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "Model": ["Word2Vec + LR", "FastText + LR", "Qwen2.5-1.5B"],
    "Type": ["Classical", "Classical", "Fine-tuned LLM"],
    "Macro-F1": [0.776, 0.773, 0.720],
    "Training Time": ["~2 min", "~2 min", "~14 min"],
    "Hardware": ["CPU (local)", "CPU (local)", "A100 (cloud)"],
    "CO2 (g)": ["~0.2", "~0.2", "~43"],
})

topic_summary["Macro-F1"] = topic_summary["Macro-F1"].map("{:.3f}".format)

styled_topic = (
    topic_summary.style
    .set_properties(**{"text-align": "center"})
    .set_table_styles([
        {"selector": "th", "props": [("text-align", "center"),
        ("background-color", "#f0f0f0")]}
    ])
)
styled_topic
```

A likely explanation for Qwen's underperformance relative to classical models is the severe
input truncation imposed during training. The median article in the dataset exceeds 1,400
tokens, yet `MAX_LENGTH` was capped at 512 tokens - meaning fewer than 1% of texts fit
within the model's context window without truncation. Classical embedding models, by contrast,
use mean-pooled representations computed over the full document, losing no content. This
structural advantage may explain why Word2Vec and FastText - which learned compact,
domain-specific co-occurrence patterns - outperformed a much larger fine-tuned LLM on this
particular task.

### Training Dynamics

The Qwen loss curves showed clean, stable convergence: training loss declined sharply from
~5.91 in the first hundred steps to ~0.39 by the end of epoch 2. Validation Macro-F1 rose
from 0.877 at the end of epoch 1 to 0.906 at the end of epoch 2, with validation loss still
decreasing (0.274 → 0.247). This indicates the model had not yet plateaued after two epochs
and would likely benefit from a third. Unlike the sentiment models (trained for 3 epochs),
Qwen was stopped early due to compute constraints.

### Label Quality Caveat for Topic

Topic labels were produced by an upstream BERT-based topic modelling pipeline, not by human
annotators. The reported metrics therefore measure agreement with that upstream model rather
than true topic accuracy. This is particularly relevant when comparing Qwen against the
classical baselines: both are learning to predict the same algorithmically derived labels,
but the classical models may exploit co-occurrence shortcuts that the topic model itself
relies on, giving them a structural edge that would not necessarily generalise to
manually validated topics.

## Embedding Model Evaluation — Gemma Embedding 300M

The experiments above concern supervised classification. A separate line of work explored
whether domain-adapted transformer embeddings could improve downstream retrieval quality for
a RAG pipeline. This section documents that experiment and its findings.

### Pretrained Baseline: Strong Out-of-the-Box Performance

Before any fine-tuning, the pretrained `gemma-embedding-300m` was evaluated by training a
logistic regression probe on its frozen embeddings. The results are striking:

```{python}
#| label: gemma-embedding-results
#| echo: true

import pandas as pd

gemma_emb = pd.DataFrame({
    "Model": [
        "gemma-embedding-300m (pretrained)",
        "gemma-embedding-300m (fine-tuned SimCSE)",
    ],
    "Sentiment Macro-F1": ["0.780", "< pretrained"],
    "Topic Macro-F1": ["0.758", "0.439 (−0.319)"],
    "Note": [
        "Best overall on both tasks",
        "Representation regression — training damaged embeddings",
    ],
})

styled_emb = (
    gemma_emb.style
    .set_properties(**{"text-align": "center"})
    .set_table_styles([
        {"selector": "th", "props": [("text-align", "center"),
        ("background-color", "#f0f0f0")]}
    ])
)
styled_emb
```

The pretrained model achieves **0.780 Macro-F1 on sentiment** and **0.758 on topic
classification** — the highest scores in the entire project on both tasks, surpassing all
fine-tuned classifiers including Gemma 2 2B (0.761 sentiment). This demonstrates that a
well-pretrained transformer embedding model, used purely as a frozen feature extractor, is a
competitive alternative to task-specific fine-tuning.

### Fine-Tuning Outcome: Representation Regression

The SimCSE fine-tuning degraded performance on both tasks. The topic classification probe
dropped by 0.319 Macro-F1 points. Intrinsic evaluation (cosine similarity gap between
synthetic positive and negative article pairs) confirmed the same direction: the positive-
negative gap *decreased* after fine-tuning, meaning the embedding space became less
well-ordered rather than more so.

Importantly, intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations moved in the same direction, validating the
use of the cosine similarity gap as a cheap proxy for downstream embedding quality.

The three most likely causes of the regression are:

1. **Learning rate too aggressive.** `1e-5` over 436,000 samples represents a very large
   cumulative parameter displacement for a model that is already strongly pretrained
   contrastively. A rate of `1e-6` or lower would have been safer.
2. **Too many gradient steps.** One full epoch over 436k chunks yields ~6,800 steps. Domain
   adaptation should be a gentle nudge — limiting to ~10-15% of the corpus with a hard
   `max_steps=2000` cap would have reduced the risk of overwriting general-purpose
   representations.
3. **Homogeneous corpus.** AI/tech journalism shares a consistent register and vocabulary,
   making in-batch SimCSE negatives trivially easy. This produces shallow gradients rather
   than genuine structural learning.

### Corrected Recipe for Future Runs

Based on the lessons from this experiment, the recommended configuration for a second attempt is:

```python
from sentence_transformers.losses import CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss

args = SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments(
    ...
    learning_rate=5e-7,           # 20× lower than original
    max_steps=2_000,              # hard cap — ~5% of original step count
    per_device_train_batch_size=128,
    batch_sampler=BatchSamplers.NO_DUPLICATES,
    ...
)
loss = CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss(model, mini_batch_size=8)

# Also: freeze the bottom half of transformer layers to prevent
# catastrophic forgetting of general-purpose representations.
```

This two-phase strategy — domain familiarisation (Phase 1, SimCSE) followed by supervised
retrieval training on query/passage pairs (Phase 2) — remains sound in principle. The failure
was in the implementation of Phase 1, not the overall design.

## Conclusion

For AI trend detection in media texts, classical Word2Vec embeddings combined with logistic
regression offer the best cost-performance ratio for both sentiment and topic classification.
Fine-tuned LLMs provide marginal improvements on sentiment at substantially higher
computational cost and carbon footprint, and did not outperform classical models on topic
classification under the conditions tested.

The most significant finding from the broader set of experiments is the performance of
pretrained `gemma-embedding-300m` as a frozen feature extractor: it outperformed every other
model on both tasks without any task-specific training. This suggests that investing in a
high-quality general-purpose embedding model may be more productive than fine-tuning smaller
models for specific tasks, at least when labelled data is limited or labels are algorithmically
derived.

The choice between approaches should be guided by the deployment context: if inference speed,
energy efficiency, and interpretability matter, classical models are the pragmatic choice.
If a unified embedding for both retrieval and classification is needed, a strong pretrained
encoder like `gemma-embedding-300m` is a compelling option. Task-specific fine-tuning of
compact LLMs is a viable path only when the accuracy gains justify the infrastructure cost
and when input truncation does not structurally disadvantage the model relative to baselines.

## Insight Extraction: What Do the Embeddings Reveal About AI Trends?

Beyond classification performance, we use the best-performing classical model (Word2Vec) to
examine the thematic structure of AI discourse. By projecting document embeddings into 2D
with UMAP and colouring by the topic labels derived in Stage 1, we can directly inspect how
topics cluster in the learned embedding space - and what this reveals about the organisation
of AI media coverage.

```{python}
#| label: insight-extraction
#| echo: true

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import umap
from pathlib import Path
from gensim.models import Word2Vec

_cwd = Path.cwd()
REPO_ROOT  = _cwd if (_cwd / "data").exists() else _cwd.parents[1]
STAGE2_DIR = REPO_ROOT / "data/processed/stage2"

# Load data and model
train = pd.read_parquet(STAGE2_DIR / "train.parquet")
test  = pd.read_parquet(STAGE2_DIR / "test.parquet")
train["tokens"] = train["tokens"].apply(eval)
test["tokens"]  = test["tokens"].apply(eval)

w2v_model = Word2Vec.load(str(STAGE2_DIR / "word2vec.model"))

def mean_pooling(tokens, model):
    vectors = [model.wv[t] for t in tokens if t in model.wv]
    return np.mean(vectors, axis=0) if vectors else np.zeros(model.vector_size)

# Combine train and test for a fuller picture
all_df = pd.concat([train, test], ignore_index=True)
all_df = all_df.dropna(subset=["topic_label"]).reset_index(drop=True)
X_all  = np.array([mean_pooling(t, w2v_model) for t in all_df["tokens"]])

# UMAP projection
reducer = umap.UMAP(n_components=2, random_state=42, n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1)
proj    = reducer.fit_transform(X_all)

# Plot coloured by topic
topics  = all_df["topic_label"].tolist()
unique_topics = sorted(set(topics))
palette = plt.cm.get_cmap("tab10", len(unique_topics))
color_map = {t: palette(i) for i, t in enumerate(unique_topics)}
colors  = [color_map[t] for t in topics]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 9))
for topic in unique_topics:
    mask = [t == topic for t in topics]
    ax.scatter(proj[mask, 0], proj[mask, 1],
               c=[color_map[topic]], s=3, alpha=0.4, label=topic)

ax.legend(markerscale=4, fontsize=8, loc="upper right",
          framealpha=0.8, title="Topic")
ax.set_title("Word2Vec Document Embeddings - UMAP projection coloured by Topic (Stage 1 labels)")
ax.set_xticks([])
ax.set_yticks([])
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The projection reveals a clear thematic organisation of AI media discourse that goes beyond
what classification metrics can capture. **Search, SEO & Marketing** (grey) forms two distinct
isolated clusters outside the main body, reflecting its highly domain-specific vocabulary
around search engines and digital marketing. **Stocks & Market Ratings** (yellow-green)
separates cleanly to the right, and **Quantum Computing** (pink) clusters at the bottom right
of the main body - both topics carry specialised terminology with little overlap with general
AI coverage. **Consumer Tech** (red) appears as a compact cluster above the main body, while
**Energy, Power & Robotics** (purple) sits at the upper left periphery. At the core,
**AI News & Tech (General)** dominates the dense centre, with **ML Models & Training Data**
heavily overlapping - consistent with the difficulty all models had separating these two
classes in classification.

Crucially, this structure was learned entirely from word co-occurrence statistics, without any
topic supervision. The fact that Word2Vec recovers the broad organisation of AI discourse
unsupervised demonstrates that classical embeddings trained on domain-specific text capture
genuine thematic structure - making them a practical tool for tracking how AI topics relate
and evolve over time.
